summary: A 1978 April 1st RFC that jokes about a Telnet option called RANDOMLY-LOSE, a mock option where one side asks permission to lose data at random. It is humorous, not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an April 1 joke document. It pretends to solve unexplained computer failures by defining a Telnet option that asks permission to lose data at random.

subtitle: An April 1 joke proposing a Telnet option to negotiate random data loss.

tldr.problem: The RFC jokes that some hosts appeared to lose data or fail without warning, confusing users.
tldr.mechanism: It pretends to define a Telnet option called RANDOMLY-LOSE that lets the peers negotiate permission to lose data.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1 joke document, not a real reliability feature or protocol recommendation.

today: RFC 748 is an April 1 joke document proposing a fictional Telnet option. It describes random lossage satirically rather than specifying a real service.

sections.title: The RANDOMLY-LOSE Option
sections.content:
RFC 748 is dated 1 April 1978 and presents a Telnet option named RANDOMLY-LOSE. It describes the option as a way for a system to request or refuse permission to lose data.

The joke's motivation is the claim that some hosts provided “random lossage,” including crashes and lost data, as part of their services.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1 joke. It treats random failures as if they were a service that a computer could offer and negotiate.

sections.title: How the Pretend Negotiation Works
sections.content:
The option uses Telnet's WILL, WON'T, DO, and DON'T negotiation commands. A server can ask permission to randomly lose data, and the user can agree or refuse; the user can also ask the server to do it.

The default is WON'T and DON'T, meaning random lossage does not happen unless negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides exchange ordinary Telnet option commands to agree or refuse. By default, the fictional loss feature is off.

sections.title: The Satirical Point
sections.content:
The memo jokes that a system that does not implement the option will be assumed to provide completely reliable uptime. This reverses the problem described in its motivation: failures that are actually unexpected are treated as a declared, negotiated feature.

The option code is 256, but the document is humorous rather than a technical recommendation.
sections.plainLanguage: The punch line is that a host without the option is supposed to be perfectly reliable. The RFC's joke is that this claim is not credible.
